name: Precentral gyrus (primary motor cortex)
func: The strip of brain just in front of the central sulcus that sends the commands for voluntary movement. Each part controls a specific body part on the opposite side of the body.

levels.kid:
The **motor cortex** is a long strip on top of your brain that goes from one ear to the other, like a headband.

It is the part that says "move!" When you kick a ball, a little spot on this strip sends a message down your spine to your leg. When you wiggle your fingers, a different spot sends the message.

Here is a funny trick: the left side of your brain moves the right side of your body, and the right side moves the left side. They cross over like an X.

Hands and lips get big spots on the strip because they do tiny, careful movements, like drawing and talking. Your back gets only a small spot.
levels.hs:
The **precentral gyrus** is the long ridge of cortex at the very back of the frontal lobe. It runs from the top of the brain near the midline down to the lateral fissure, and continues onto the medial surface as part of the **paracentral lobule**. Directly behind it is the **central sulcus**, and just behind that is the postcentral gyrus, which handles touch. Movement and feeling are neighbors.

The precentral gyrus is the **primary motor cortex**. Its neurons send axons down through the brain and spinal cord in the **corticospinal tract**. About 85–90% of those fibers cross to the other side in the lower medulla (the pyramidal decussation), so each hemisphere controls the opposite side of the body.

The body is mapped onto the gyrus in order, a pattern drawn as the **motor homunculus** ("little man"), first mapped by Wilder Penfield in the 1930s–50s by stimulating patients' brains during surgery. The legs and feet are on the medial surface near the midline, then going down the side of the brain come the trunk, arm, hand, face, lips and tongue. The hand and face areas are huge compared with their real size because they need fine control.
levels.college:
The primary motor cortex corresponds to **Brodmann area 4**. In front of it lies BA 6, the premotor cortex laterally and the **supplementary motor area (SMA)** medially. The **hand knob**, an omega- or epsilon-shaped bulge of the precentral gyrus seen on axial MRI, reliably marks the hand area.

Output runs from layer V pyramidal neurons, including the giant **Betz cells**, through the corona radiata and the **posterior limb of the internal capsule**, then the cerebral peduncles, basis pontis and medullary pyramids. Most fibers cross at the pyramidal decussation to form the **lateral corticospinal tract**; the uncrossed remainder runs in the anterior corticospinal tract to axial muscles. Fibers to cranial nerve motor nuclei leave as **corticobulbar** fibers, and most cranial motor nuclei receive input from both hemispheres. The key exception is the lower face, which gets mainly crossed input.

Only part of the corticospinal tract actually comes from area 4: roughly a third, with the rest from premotor, SMA and parietal cortex.

Blood supply follows the homunculus: the **anterior cerebral artery** supplies the medial leg and foot area, and the **middle cerebral artery** supplies the lateral face, arm and hand areas. That is why an MCA stroke weakens the face and arm more than the leg, while an ACA stroke mainly weakens the leg.

Input arrives from the premotor cortex and SMA, from the somatosensory cortex via U-fibers across the central sulcus, and from the cerebellum and basal ganglia through the ventral lateral and ventral anterior nuclei of the thalamus.
levels.phd:
Motor cortex neurons encode movement as a population. Georgopoulos showed that each neuron has a **preferred direction** and fires broadly around it; summing neuron "votes" weighted by firing rate gives a **population vector** that predicts the direction of reach. This principle underlies **brain-computer interfaces**, in which implanted microelectrode arrays in the motor cortex of people with paralysis decode intended movements to control cursors or robotic arms.

Newer work treats motor cortex as a **dynamical system**: during preparation, population activity settles into an initial state, and movement unfolds as rotational trajectories through neural state space (Churchland and Shenoy).

Only a minority of corticospinal neurons in primates make **direct corticomotoneuronal (CM) connections** onto spinal motor neurons. These direct connections are concentrated on hand muscles and are especially well developed in humans and great apes, enabling independent finger movements. Most corticospinal fibers end on spinal interneurons.

The map is less clean than the classic homunculus. Within the arm area, maps overlap and are organized partly by **ethologically relevant actions**, such as hand-to-mouth or defensive postures, as shown with long-train stimulation by Graziano. A 2023 study (Gordon and colleagues) proposed that effector regions are separated by **inter-effector** zones linked to whole-body action planning; this idea is still being tested.

The map is **plastic**: practice enlarges the cortical representation of the trained movement, and after amputation or nerve injury neighboring areas take over the territory. Inhibitory **GABAergic interneurons** sharpen output, and reduced GABA signaling after stroke is thought to open a window for recovery through rehabilitation.
levels.expert:
A lesion of the primary motor cortex causes **contralateral weakness** in an **upper motor neuron** pattern. Acutely, tone may be low ("cerebral shock"); over days to weeks, **spasticity** (velocity-dependent, "clasp-knife"), **hyperreflexia**, clonus and an extensor plantar response (**Babinski sign**) develop. Weakness favors the arm extensors and leg flexors (the **pyramidal distribution**). A subtle sign is **pronator drift**: with arms held out palms up and eyes closed, the weak arm pronates and drifts down.

Because cortical territory is spread out, small cortical lesions cause weakness of just part of the body, such as a hand or face, while a lesion in the internal capsule, where the fibers are packed tightly, causes face, arm and leg weakness together. **Central facial palsy** spares the forehead because the upper face has input from both hemispheres; this separates it from a facial nerve (Bell's) palsy, which paralyzes the whole side.

**Focal motor seizures** start here. In a **Jacksonian march**, jerking spreads in homunculus order, for example from the fingers to the hand, arm and face. After a seizure, temporary weakness called **Todd's paralysis** can mimic stroke.

**Imaging:** MRI locates the hand knob. Functional MRI and **navigated transcranial magnetic stimulation** map motor areas before surgery, and **diffusion tensor tractography** shows the corticospinal tract.

**Surgery:** tumors near the motor strip (rolandic gliomas, convexity meningiomas) are removed with intraoperative **direct cortical and subcortical stimulation** and **motor evoked potential** monitoring to preserve function. The **phase reversal** of somatosensory evoked potentials across the central sulcus identifies it in the operating room. Motor cortex stimulation has also been used for some chronic pain syndromes.

keyPoints: Primary motor cortex = Brodmann area 4, just in front of the central sulcus
Somatotopic map: leg medial (ACA), face and hand lateral (MCA)
Corticospinal tract crosses in the lower medulla → contralateral control
Lesion → UMN signs: spasticity, hyperreflexia, Babinski
Central facial palsy spares the forehead

test.q: Where on the motor homunculus is the leg represented?
choices: Lateral surface near the lateral fissure
test.explain: The leg and foot are on the medial surface in the paracentral lobule, supplied by the ACA.

test.q: The giant layer V pyramidal neurons of the primary motor cortex are called ______ cells.
test.explain: Betz cells are the largest neurons in the cortex, though they form only a small fraction of corticospinal fibers.

test.q: An MCA stroke typically causes weakness that is worst in:
choices: Face and arm more than leg
test.explain: The MCA supplies the lateral motor strip, where the face, arm and hand are represented.

test.q: A left motor cortex lesion causes a facial weakness that:
choices: Involves the whole right face including the forehead
Affects the lower right face and spares the forehead
test.explain: The upper face gets input from both hemispheres, so a central lesion spares the forehead on the opposite side.

test.q: Seizure jerking that spreads from the hand to the arm to the face in homunculus order is called a ______ march.
test.explain: Named after John Hughlings Jackson, it reflects seizure spread across the motor map.

test.q: Where do most corticospinal fibers cross the midline?
test.explain: About 85–90% cross at the pyramidal decussation in the lower medulla.
